summary: This Wikipedia article describes excoriation disorder (dermatillomania), a mental disorder on the obsessive-compulsive spectrum characterized by repeated urges to pick at one's own skin causing psychological or physical damage. It covers signs and symptoms, complications, proposed causes including neurological and genetic factors, diagnostic debates around its DSM-5 classification, similarities to OCD, trichotillomania and addiction, and pharmacological treatments. The page is cut off before the psychological treatment section.
one_line: Wikipedia overview of excoriation disorder (dermatillomania), a body-focused compulsive skin-picking disorder covering symptoms, causes, diagnosis and medication treatments.
key_facts: Excoriation disorder, more commonly known as dermatillomania, is a mental disorder on the obsessive-compulsive spectrum characterized by the repeated urge or impulse to pick at one's own skin.
The face is the region most commonly picked, though frequent locations include the arms, legs, back, gums, neck, shoulders, scalp, abdomen, chest, and fingernails.
In one reported case, a woman picked a hole through the bridge of her nose, which required surgery to fix.
A 48-year-old woman picked through the skin on her neck, exposing the carotid artery.
Studies have shown excoriation disorder presented suicidal ideation in 12% of individuals, suicide attempts in 11.5%, and psychiatric hospitalizations in 15%.
Studies have shown a linkage between dopamine and the urge to pick; cocaine and methamphetamine, which increase dopamine effects, have been shown to cause uncontrollable picking in users.
A significant link was found between a single nucleotide polymorphism within the SAPAP3 gene and trichotillomania.
As of the DSM-5 released in May 2013, excoriation (skin-picking) disorder is classified as its own separate condition under 'Obsessive Compulsive and Related Disorders'.

The Diagnostic Interview for Skin Picking Problems (DISP) was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health in May 2022; 88% of 120 participants were identified as meeting DSM-5 criteria.
A review by Jenkins et al. concluded that a separate DSM-5 category for excoriation disorder requires more evidence.
Odlaug and Grant suggested excoriation disorder is more akin to substance use disorder than OCD.
One study found 79% of patients with excoriation disorder reported a pleasurable feeling when picking.
Only 45% of individuals with excoriation disorder ever sought treatment, and only 19% ever received dermatological treatment, in one study.
A meta-analysis found SSRIs and lamotrigine were no more effective than placebo for long-term effects.
Medications reported as possibly effective in reducing picking include doxepin, clomipramine, naltrexone, pimozide, and olanzapine.
Topiramate, an anti-epileptic drug, was found in a small study of individuals with Prader–Willi syndrome to reduce skin picking.
